title: Catullus 8: the poem and this translation
short: A soliloquy in which Catullus orders himself to stop loving Lesbia; Robinson Ellis (1871) imitates the 'limping' iambic metre.
body: In poem 8 Catullus speaks to himself as miser Catulle, 'wretched Catullus', and tells himself to give up a mistress who no longer wants him. Merrill dates it to about 59 BC, during a quarrel, and is sure the girl is Lesbia. Ellis's commentary notes how often Catullus addresses himself and uses his own name. The metre is the choliambus or scazon ('limping iambic'), an iambic line whose last foot is reversed, so that it seems to stumble at the close. Robinson Ellis's translation (1871) uses long iambic lines, many ending in a heavy pair of stresses ('no more', 'is past'). The archive keeps his indentations, which mark the poem's sections.

title: 'learn to play the fool no more'
short: Ineptire, 'to act foolishly', is a colloquial word from comedy; the subjunctive desinas is a firm self-instruction.
body: The Latin desinas ineptire means 'you are to stop playing the fool'. Merrill points out that ineptire is colloquial: it appears twice in Terence, never in Plautus, and in no classical author after Catullus. Ellis's commentary reads desinas as a hortatory subjunctive laying down a rule of conduct, rather than a plain command. The vocabulary of the comic stage matters to the poem's tone, since lovesick young men in Plautus and Terence are told the same things by their slaves. Ellis's 'learn to play the fool no more' is close, and the added 'learn' anticipates the poem's final line.

title: 'Lost is the lost'
greek: et quod vides perisse perditum ducas
short: 'Count as lost what you see is lost': a proverbial phrase modelled on Plautus.
body: The Latin is et quod vides perisse perditum ducas, 'and what you see has perished, count as lost'. Merrill and Ellis both trace it to Plautus, Trinummus 1026, quin tu quod periit periisse ducis?, a commonplace of comic common sense. Ellis notes that perire and perdere were often set side by side as passive and active. His translation, 'Lost is the lost', keeps the jingle of the two forms and makes it proverbial. The second half, 'and the past is past', is Ellis's own doubling. It fits the poem's theme of past happiness set against present loss.

title: 'Bright once the days and sunny shone the light on thee'
short: 'Bright suns once shone for you': the white or shining day was a Greek and Roman image of happiness.
body: Catullus writes fulsere quondam candidi tibi soles, 'once the bright suns shone for you'. Merrill explains candidi soles as days of good fortune and contrasts Horace's 'black sun' of a bad day (Satires 1.9.72). Ellis cites Aeschylus's 'white day' (Persians 301) and Sophocles' use of a 'white' day for a lucky one. The line is repeated as a refrain at line 8 with vere ('truly') replacing quondam ('once'). Ellis's English spends a whole long line on it, with both 'Bright' and 'sunny' standing for candidi.

anchor: Still ever hasting where she led
title: 'Still ever hasting where she led'
short: The frequentative ventitabas ('you kept going') shows the lover always following where his mistress led.
body: The Latin cum ventitabas quo puella ducebat means 'when you used to keep going wherever the girl led'. Ventitare is a frequentative, so the action was repeated. Merrill says it refers not to a particular house but to the lover's whole submission to her guidance. Ellis agrees that ducebat ('led the way') implies Catullus's surrender to her will, not any trick on her part. The image of the lover as a follower recurs at line 10, where he is told not to follow one who runs away. Ellis's 'Still ever hasting' gives the repetition well. 'Hasting', an archaic form of 'hastening', adds eagerness.

anchor: as maiden is belov'd no more
title: 'By me belov'd as maiden is belov'd no more'
short: 'Loved by me as no girl will ever be loved': Catullus makes the same boast elsewhere about Lesbia.
body: The Latin amata nobis quantum amabitur nulla means 'loved by us as much as none will be loved'. Merrill uses this line to identify the girl, since Catullus makes the same claim for Lesbia in poems 37 and 87. The plural nobis ('by us') is a common poetic plural for 'by me'. The future amabitur makes the claim reach into all time. Ellis keeps the doubled verb ('belov'd ... belov'd') and uses the archaic 'maid' for puella throughout. His 'no more' gives the Latin future a backward look, as though the speaker already knows the love is over.

anchor: the maid she said not nay
title: 'the maid she said not nay'
greek: quae tu volebas nec puella nolebat
short: A litotes: what he wanted, the girl 'did not not want'. The understatement is playful and a little rueful.
body: Lines 6-7 describe the playful love of the past: ibi illa multa cum iocosa fiebant, / quae tu volebas nec puella nolebat, 'then those many playful things were done, which you wanted and the girl did not refuse'. The figure is litotes, assertion by a denied negative: volebas ... nec nolebat. Merrill compares Ovid's description of his own Muse as iocosa. Ellis renders iocosa, with its erotic undertone, as 'the merry mirth'. He keeps the litotes in 'she said not nay', an old ballad idiom, while 'enacting' is a slightly theatrical choice for fiebant ('were done').

title: The refrain
short: Line 3 returns with 'truly' for 'once', closing the memory of past joy; line 11's 'endure' returns in the same way at line 19.
body: Line 8 repeats line 3 with one word changed: vere ('truly') for quondam ('once'). Merrill describes the poem's structure: the past is framed by these two lines, and the resolve for the future is framed by line 11 (obstinata mente perfer, obdura) and the last line (at tu, Catulle, destinatus obdura). He notes the small variation in each pair, quondam/vere and obstinata/destinatus. Ellis keeps both refrains clearly. His layout sets the refrain lines at the left margin and many of the lines between them indented, so the ring structure can be seen.

anchor: child, do thou resign no less
title: 'child, do thou resign no less'
greek: nunc iam illa non volt: tu quoque impotens noli
short: Latin impotens ('without self-control') is the transmitted reading; Ellis renders it 'child', the weak lover told to stop wanting.
body: Line 9 reads nunc iam illa non volt: tu quoque impotens noli, 'now she no longer wants; you too, powerless one, must not want'. Impotens is the reading of the manuscripts, not an emendation; the question is what it means here. It can mean 'weak, without power over oneself', a man ruled by his passions, and that is the sense most editors give it, though it is a stronger word than a plain 'weakling'. The play between volt ('she wills') and noli ('do not will') answers the volebas ... nolebat of line 7. Ellis's 'child' renders impotens as helpless immaturity. His 'resigns ... resign' substitutes his own wordplay on giving up for Catullus's willing and unwilling.

anchor: Nor follow her that flies thee
title: 'Nor follow her that flies thee'
short: 'Don't chase the one who runs away': a proverb found in Theocritus, whom Catullus may be recalling.
body: The Latin is nec quae fugit sectare, nec miser vive, 'do not chase her who flees, and do not live in misery'. Merrill compares Theocritus 11.75, where the Cyclops asks himself why he chases the one who runs from him. He thinks Catullus may have had that passage in mind, though in Theocritus the words keep more of their literal meaning. The Cyclops, a ridiculous lovelorn monster, is an ironic model for a poet trying to be firm. The line also reverses the image of line 4, where Catullus went where the girl led. Ellis's 'or to bide in woe consent' turns nec miser vive into a refusal to accept misery.

anchor: harden all thy heart, resolve, endure
title: 'harden all thy heart, resolve, endure'
short: Two blunt imperatives without a joining word: 'bear it through, be hard'. Ovid later borrows the phrase.
body: The Latin is sed obstinata mente perfer, obdura, 'but with a stubborn mind, bear it out, be hard'. Merrill notes that the asyndeton (no 'and' between the imperatives) gives the line a rugged determination. He also notes that Ovid reuses the phrase (Tristia 5.11.7, perfer et obdura) and that Horace has persta atque obdura (Satires 2.5.39). Obdurare is literally 'to harden'. Ellis translates it twice, in 'harden' and 'endure', and adds 'resolve'. His triad then comes back in the next line and at the end of the poem, so it becomes a refrain of its own.

title: The shift to the third person
short: Catullus says farewell and speaks of himself as 'Catullus', as if he were already the firm man he wants to be.
body: Line 12 reads vale, puella. iam Catullus obdurat, 'goodbye, girl. Now Catullus is hard'. Merrill draws attention to the change of person: the poet has been addressing himself as 'you' and now speaks of 'Catullus' in the third person, before returning to 'you' at line 19. Ellis lists the many places where Catullus names himself. Readers disagree whether the third person here sounds like real self-mastery or like a man acting a part and watching himself do it. Ellis's 'Catullus is resolv'd, endures' keeps the switch. Note that in his version 'Farewell, my love' is warmer than the Latin's plain vale, puella.

title: 'will not importune'
greek: nec te requiret nec rogabit invitam
short: He will not seek her or ask for her against her will; 'importune' means to beg persistently.
body: The Latin is nec te requiret nec rogabit invitam, 'he will not seek you or ask you when you are unwilling'. Rogare ('to ask') is used, as often in love poetry, for asking a woman's favours. Merrill notes that in line 14 rogaberis is used in the same way, without saying what is asked for. That line turns the word round: she will grieve when nobody asks her (rogaberis nulla). Ellis renders the second verb as 'importune', 'to pester with requests' (OED). His clause 'He will not ask for pity' adds a sentiment that is not in the Latin.

title: 'O past retrieval faithless! Ah what hours are thine!'
greek: scelesta, vae te, quae tibi manet vita?
short: Scelesta, 'wicked woman', and vae te, 'woe to you': anger turns at once into a picture of the life left to her.
body: Line 15 reads scelesta, vae te, quae tibi manet vita?, 'wretch, woe to you, what life remains for you?' Merrill notes that vae is usually followed by a dative, but an accusative of exclamation is also found in comedy. He takes tibi manet as 'will continue to be yours', not 'awaits you'. He observes that Catullus 'fans his anger' but at once dwells on details of past happiness, as if to tempt her back. Ellis renders scelesta as 'past retrieval faithless', a moral judgement stronger than the Latin, and he turns the question about her life into 'what hours are thine'.

title: The string of questions
short: Six questions picture her future lovers; the last, about whose lips she will bite, is the most physical and the most telling.
body: Lines 16-18 run: quis nunc te adibit? cui videberis bella? / quem nunc amabis? cuius esse diceris? / quem basiabis? cui labella mordebis?, 'who will come to you now? to whom will you seem pretty? whom will you love? whose will you be called? whom will you kiss? whose lips will you bite?' Merrill reads the questions as showing that Catullus does not yet suspect a rival, and he cites love-bites in Plautus, Horace (Odes 1.13.12) and Tibullus. The questions move from the social to the erotic, and the poet's resolve seems to weaken as he goes. Ellis's renderings are free: 'who decrees to live thine own?' is a loose version of cuius esse diceris ('whose will you be called?').

title: The last line
short: The poem ends where line 11 did, with the order to be hard; destinatus, 'determined', is a new sense of the word.
body: The last line is at tu, Catulle, destinatus obdura, 'but you, Catullus, be determined and hard'. Merrill notes that this is the first use of destinatus in the sense of obstinatus ('resolute'), and that it varies the obstinata of line 11, just as vere varies quondam in the first refrain. The return to 'you' after the third-person 'Catullus' of line 12 suggests that the resolve has to be made again. Ellis's 'Yet, yet' doubles the adversative at, and his closing triad 'bear, resolve, endure' completes the series he began at line 11.

title: How serious is the poem?
short: Critics divide between reading the poem as real heartbreak and as a lover's self-mockery in the manner of Roman comedy.
body: Much of the poem's vocabulary (ineptire, perisse perditum, vae te) comes, as Merrill's notes show, from Plautus and Terence. There the lovesick young man is a stock comic figure who is told to be firm and never manages it. Merrill himself thought the poet 'ill able' to bear Lesbia's coldness with dignity and saw him keeping one eye open for reconciliation. A. L. Wheeler, following E. P. Morris, took the poem as a comic exercise, and Marilyn Skinner (1971) read the speaker as a comic lover ironically aware of his role. Fordyce, Fraenkel and Quinn instead treat it as a serious study of inner conflict, as P. J. Connor's survey (1974) sets out. Ellis's earnest, archaic English leans towards the serious reading.
